Unity felt consistent, usable and boring - qualities I appreciate in a DE. It set Ubuntu apart and by the time of migration away from it was actually pretty stable and solid.
Unity was probably the most straightforward n00b-friendly Linux DE. Still rocking it in 2022 on a 16.06 Ubuntu image - less objectionable than GNOME and less fiddly than KDE.
The killer feature of Unity is the HUD allowing you to simply type to find menu items. Saves so much time going through options.
Canonical had two variants of Unity, the regular one (slow) and a qml based one (super snappy). Still sad they didn't stick with the qml version - GNOME was slow and lacking for years compared to it.
Unity's global menu system was wonderful and used vertical space well; switching to GNOME was like going back 10 years with multiple empty bars and random scattered icons.
I remember quitting Ubuntu because they dropped Unity.
I have never understood Unity. For all its faults I never once considered GNOME, KDE, or Cinnamon inferior to it; features Unity had were implemented and superseded by GNOME long ago.

When Ubuntu moved to GNOME shell with their customizations, it felt strange for a couple hours, then everything made sense - icons are where they used to be, not much really feels different from stock GNOME.
Unity was OK once the global menu was disabled. Today I use KDE - it lets me configure it the way I want.
Compiz kick started the belief that Linux 'Year of the Desktop' could be a real thing. Wobbly windows, fire and the cube were great demos to get people interested in Linux.
Using Ubuntu/Compiz for a couple years, it has annoying quirks e.g. child windows popping up on the wrong monitor - thank goodness for WIN+SHIFT+arrow keys - but no desire to go back to Windows 10/8.
Compiz seems not to be actively maintained since 2016; development suddenly stopped despite its past fame.
I used Compiz with 17.04 and it was nice, but decided to try native GNOME with 18.04 after a reinstall. Not perfect but does the job, and didn't want to install something unmaintained.

I still remember when GNOME 2 reached its peak with Ubuntu in the early 2000s - complete, reliable, configurable, robust. Everything since has been downhill, with new features at the expense of no-frills functional design.
With just Ubuntu, very few games, mediocre graphics card drivers, and a painful interface like Unity (try hiding/unhiding/switching between hidden windows), it's hard to convince myself to buy this.
Don't bother - the Alienware Ubuntu box's Nvidia GTX 645 wants you to use proprietary driver blobs without any source code.
I have but one wish: when I open the Dash and type 'calc' to launch Calculator, LibreOffice Calc has higher priority, so I always have to select it specifically instead of pressing Enter.
Left Ubuntu because of some bloatware/opinionated stuff and it crashed a lot; I like Antergos with i3-gnome better - much better performance, fewer crashes/bugs.
Ubuntu works for me and my wife and has for years. I pine for the days of GNOME 2 but that's not coming back. If Unity could be made into GNOME 2 but keep Unity people happy that would be cool.
Google is a paying customer for Canonical's Ubuntu Advantage support program, though Chris Kenyon noted Google is not their largest business desktop customer.
